clue.text: Penelope Fitzgerald's book agent

parts.note: in Fitzgerald's novel At ..., the title character runs a London stage school and acts as agent for its child actors

explanation.surface: A question about who handled a novelist's publishing deals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book agent' reads as a literary agent who sells manuscripts; here it is an agent inside one of her books, the woman who places child actors in At Freddie's.
explanation.definitionFit: The title figure of At Freddie's runs a theatrical school and finds stage work for her pupils, an agent within the novel.

clue.text: Brookner book with point for dubious types

parts.note: Fraud is a 1992 novel by Anita Brookner
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A novel by Anita Brookner, plus something extra, describes shady characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheats and impostors are dubious characters.

clue.text: Sailors patron in Balearic resort

explanation.surface: A seafarers' saint is honoured at a Mediterranean holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Saint Eulalia of Barcelona is invoked by seafarers, and Santa Eulalia des Riu is a resort town on Ibiza.
explanation.definitionFit: The Barcelona martyr is a protector of seafarers, and her name forms part of the Ibiza town Santa Eulalia.

clue.text: Relatively inactive Shavian waste-disposal operative

explanation.surface: An idle character from Shaw who empties bins.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred, father of Eliza in Shaw's Pygmalion, is a dustman (a refuse collector); the first sense is the phrase 'do little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who does little is relatively idle; Shaw's Alfred in Pygmalion works as a dustman, a refuse collector.

clue.text: Mistakenly assume hints will reveal special interests of Robertson Davies

indicators.note: letters taken mistakenly are set out in the wrong order, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wrongly reading clues will expose what a Canadian novelist cared about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Enthusiasms of Robertson Davies' is a collection of the Canadian novelist's essays.
explanation.definitionFit: Passions or keen interests, as in the title of the collection of Davies's writings.

clue.text: "Strew me the ground with Daffadowndillies,/ And Cowslips, and Cowslips, and loved lilies " (Spenser)

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as a Spenser quotation reading 'And Cowslips, and Cowslips, and loved lilies': the gap where the missing word belongs has been filled with a repeat of 'Cowslips', so the clue as held does not define the answer
annotationWithheld.clue: "Strew me the ground with Daffadowndillies,/ And Cowslips, and Cowslips, and loved lilies " (Spenser)

clue.text: Maxwell Anderson's was broad and slow

definitions.text: Maxwell Anderson's was broad and slow

parts.words: Maxwell Anderson's was broad and slow
parts.note: Maxwell Anderson wrote the play ... Largo, and largo is the musical direction meaning broad and slow

explanation.surface: A remark about the pace of an American playwright's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word comes before 'Largo' in the title of Anderson's 1939 play; 'largo' in music means broad and slow.
explanation.definitionFit: The play title is completed by the word before Largo, the tempo marking for a broad, slow pace.

clue.text: Tangled skein of cursive writing ()

indicators.note: a tangled skein of wool has its strands muddled, so the word's letters are muddled too

explanation.surface: A knotted ball of yarn resembles flowing handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: Naskhi or neskhi is a rounded, flowing Arabic script, a cursive hand.

clue.text: Poet gives credit to a playwright

parts.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist

explanation.surface: A verse writer acknowledges a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Crashaw was a seventeenth-century English metaphysical poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Crashaw wrote devotional metaphysical verse.

clue.text: Basic theory of normal ten cents worth, say

parts.note: par is the normal or standard level

indicators.note: say means the following words are spoken and the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: a dime is a US coin worth ten cents

explanation.surface: A discussion of a basic theory valued at only a few cents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' tells you the pronunciation: 'a dime' sounds like the end of the word, spelt ADIGM.
explanation.definitionFit: A model or framework of thought underlying a science is its fundamental theory.

clue.text: Entirely admirable Fielding squire

parts.note: all means entirely, as in 'all alone'
worthy means deserving respect, admirable

explanation.surface: A wholly good country gentleman from an eighteenth-century novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Squire Allworthy is Tom's benevolent guardian in Fielding's Tom Jones; the name describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: The kindly squire who raises the foundling hero of Tom Jones.

clue.text: Celestial body said to be associated with Mrs Herries ()

indicators.note: said to be means the word is spoken, so its sound counts but not its spelling

parts.note: a star is a heavenly body

explanation.surface: A heavenly body linked by report with a character from a family saga.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hugh Walpole's Rogue Herries, the gypsy Mirabell Starr becomes the second wife of Francis Herries.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirabell, wife of Francis Herries in Walpole's saga, was born with this surname.

clue.text: No longer quiet oracle's retreat in India…

indicators.note: no longer quiet means the word loses its quiet letter, the musical symbol for soft

parts.note: Delphi in Greece was the seat of Apollo's oracle
p, piano, is the musical direction meaning quiet

explanation.surface: An oracle's sanctuary that has lost its peace, somewhere in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer quiet' removes P from DELPHI.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital territory is a city in the north of the subcontinent.

clue.text: … where a Hindu spa conceals holy book?

indicators.note: conceals means the letters are disguised by being jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A Hindu bathing place hides sacred scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues the previous one with its ellipsis. 'Conceals' suggests a hidden word, but the letters of the three words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Upanishads are ancient Sanskrit scriptures of Hindu philosophy.

clue.text: After combat, deadly epidemic for this Nobel prizewinner

definitions.text: After combat, deadly epidemic for this Nobel prizewinner

parts.words: After combat, deadly epidemic for this Nobel prizewinner
parts.note: the writer edited the Resistance newspaper Combat and then published the novel La Peste (The Plague)

explanation.surface: A laureate who followed fighting with a plague.
explanation.walkthrough: Combat was the French Resistance paper this writer edited; 'deadly epidemic' points to The Plague (1947). He won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1957.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-Algerian author edited Combat, wrote The Plague and won the 1957 Nobel Prize for Literature.

clue.text: Officer providing transportation for Mr Pickwick

definitions.text: Officer providing transportation for Mr Pickwick

parts.words: Officer providing transportation for Mr Pickwick
parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers a landowner with a military title finds the sleeping Pickwick in a wheelbarrow and has him wheeled off to the pound

explanation.surface: An army man arranging travel for a Dickens hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transportation' suggests a coach or carriage, or even deportation; Pickwick is in fact trundled to the village pound in a wheelbarrow on the officer's orders.
explanation.definitionFit: The bad-tempered landowner in Pickwick Papers, with a naval rank, orders the trespassing Pickwick wheeled away in a barrow.

clue.text: Reportedly not a weighty reason for a repeated idea

indicators.note: reportedly means the phrase is heard rather than seen, so only its sound matters

parts.note: light means not weighty, and a motive is a reason

explanation.surface: A trivial excuse for returning to a theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light motive' said aloud gives the German-derived musical term, spelt LEITMOTIV.
explanation.definitionFit: A recurring theme in music or literature, associated with a character or idea.

clue.text: Splendid one-word critique of Wodehouse oeuvre

explanation.surface: A one-word rave review of P. G. Wodehouse's comic novels.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is old-fashioned British slang for excellent, of the kind Wodehouse's characters use.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated British slang for excellent, and a word fitting both the style and the merit of Wodehouse's books.

clue.text: Mrs Badger's second choice was academic racket game

parts.note: a professor is a senior university academic
a din is a loud noise, a racket
go is the Japanese board game

explanation.surface: A lecturer as a woman's second pick, or a game played with rackets.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Bleak House, Mrs Bayham Badger lists her three husbands, the second being this professor. 'Racket game' suggests tennis or squash.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Bayham Badger in Bleak House married three times, and this scholar was her second husband.

clue.text: Lady Nicholson inspired him, or her

definitions.text: Lady Nicholson inspired him, or her

parts.words: Lady Nicholson inspired him, or her
parts.note: Vita Sackville-West, wife of Sir Harold Nicolson, was the model for Virginia Woolf's hero who changes sex partway through the novel

explanation.surface: A titled woman who was the muse of a man, or perhaps a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Vita Sackville-West was Lady Nicolson by marriage; Woolf's 1928 novel about her has a hero who lives for centuries and wakes up a woman, hence 'him, or her'.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's title character, modelled on Vita Sackville-West, begins life as a man and becomes a woman.

clue.text: Georgia doctor with nothing on gets silver decoration

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
O, the figure zero, means nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Georgian doctor wearing nothing receives a piece of silverware.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative edging of fluting or beading on silverware.

clue.text: "Words of learned, and thundering sound / Amazed the gazing rustics rang'd around" (Goldsmith)

definitions.text: "Words of learned, and thundering sound / Amazed the gazing rustics rang'd around" (Goldsmith)

parts.words: "Words of learned, and thundering sound / Amazed the gazing rustics rang'd around" (Goldsmith)
parts.note: the couplet from Goldsmith's The Deserted Village, about the schoolmaster, lacks one noun after 'learned'

explanation.surface: Lines describing a village schoolmaster dazzling his rural listeners with long words.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from The Deserted Village (1770); the gap after 'learned' takes the missing noun, giving 'words of learned ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldsmith's schoolmaster used words of great size and duration, long words that awed the villagers.

clue.text: Some pieces in oral tradition transform sumo flick

indicators.note: to transform is to change shape, so the letters are reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: A film about Japanese wrestling being reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional songs and tunes passed on by ear rather than in writing.

clue.text: Ponders inspirational women ()

explanation.surface: Someone thinks about the goddesses who inspire artists.
explanation.definitionFit: To muse is to reflect or think deeply; the nine Greek goddesses of arts and learning inspired poets.

clue.text: Deranged German on ecstasy identifies Mass Observer

parts.note: mad means deranged
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A crazed German on drugs picks out a social researcher.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Madge co-founded Mass-Observation, the British project recording everyday life from 1937.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Madge, poet and sociologist, was a founder of the Mass-Observation social research project.

clue.text: Mary Roberts Rinehart's Rachel returns, in her chosen nightie

indicators.note: returns means the letters found are read back the other way
in means the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A character comes back wearing the nightdress she picked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points inside 'chosen nightie', where SENNI runs across the word join; 'returns' turns it round. Rachel Innes narrates Rinehart's The Circular Staircase.
explanation.definitionFit: Rachel Innes is the spinster narrator of The Circular Staircase.

clue.text: Powerful-sounding women's writer's women's writer

parts.note: the surname sounds like a strong limb, and it belongs to a critic who writes about women's writing

explanation.surface: A forceful-sounding author who writes about other women authors.
explanation.walkthrough: The name splits into two words suggesting muscle; Isobel and Nancy of this surname are scholars of women's writing, so a 'women's writer's writer' in both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A surname implying a mighty limb, borne by critics of fiction by and for women.

clue.text: Stevenson's pretty beastly travelling companion

parts.note: in Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes, Robert Louis Stevenson walks with a she-donkey called Modestine

explanation.surface: A novelist's rather unpleasant fellow traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty beastly' sounds like mild disapproval; it is literal, as the companion is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Modestine, the donkey Stevenson led through the Cévennes, is a beast of burden of this kind.

clue.text: Cosmetic aids to deeper understanding?

parts.note: the word means both shiny lip cosmetics and explanatory notes added to a text

explanation.surface: Asking whether makeup helps one understand things better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cosmetic aids' points to make-up for the lips; 'aids to deeper understanding' points to commentary written in a text's margins. The one word does both.
explanation.definitionFit: Lip cosmetics and marginal explanatory notes share this word.

clue.text: Hillier's hill

parts.note: the American poet Robert Hillyer published the collection The ... Hill in 1928

explanation.surface: A hill belonging to someone with a fitting name.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet's name is usually spelt Hillyer; his book The Seventh Hill gives the word before 'Hill'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinal number in the title of Hillyer's poetry collection The Seventh Hill.
